output.executive_summary: The September 2026 brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods using satellite land-surface temperature measurements from July afternoons in 2023–2025. It found that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density; impervious surface was the strongest single predictor [S1][S2][S3]. Heat-related emergency calls were 23% higher in the hottest neighborhood quartile than in the coolest [S3]. The authors recommend prioritizing tree planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide 30% canopy-cover target by 2035, while noting that the study demonstrates association rather than causation [S4].
output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026 and authored by Dr. Amara Nwosu and Kenji Morita of the Riverton Institute for Urban Studies, describes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. The study found that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says these findings support targeted planting in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

Canopy cover was measured from 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41%. The researchers derived land-surface temperature from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, each between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. They used a multiple regression model with average afternoon land-surface temperature as the outcome and canopy cover, impervious-surface share, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy cover, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy cover, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C. The difference was 6.4°C. Impervious-surface share was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, followed by canopy cover. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The brief cautions that land-surface temperature is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design establishes association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The authors estimate that planting 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].

output.detailed_summary:
The report covers July 1 to September 30, 2026, was prepared by Elena Vasquez, Project Manager, Harbor City Public Library, and is dated October 6, 2026. It assigns the project an overall status of Amber: go-live remains on schedule, but the project is over budget. As of the report, migration to the new platform provided by Larkspur Data Services LLC was 85% complete, with 412,000 of 485,000 catalog records migrated. The planned go-live date is November 17, 2026, when public access to the legacy catalog will also end [S1].

Quarterly highlights were completion of data mapping on July 24, 2026, completion of a pilot migration at the Central branch on August 28, 2026, and usability testing of the new patron search interface, which passed with 18 volunteer patrons [S1]. The approved budget is $180,000; spending was $112,400 as of September 30, 2026. The forecast at completion is $186,500, or $6,500 above the approved budget, mainly due to additional data-cleanup work [S2].

The milestone information lists data mapping and pilot migration as complete on July 24, 2026 and August 28, 2026, respectively; staff training is in progress, with a due date of November 3, 2026; and go-live is planned for November 17, 2026. On September 9, 2026, the steering committee approved extending the pilot to two additional branch libraries, Eastgate and Millbrook [S2].

The report identifies a risk that duplicate bibliographic records from the legacy system may delay go-live. Tomas Lindqvist, Data Lead, owns this risk, and a deduplication script is to be run by October 20, 2026. A second risk is that Larkspur's lead migration engineer is leaving the vendor in November 2026; the project has requested a written staffing transition plan from Larkspur [S3]. Listed actions are for Elena Vasquez to circulate the revised staff training schedule by October 10, 2026; Tomas Lindqvist to deliver the deduplication report by October 20, 2026; and Finance to confirm contingency funding of $6,500 by October 31, 2026 [S3].

output.executive_summary: The brief reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods using satellite measurements from July 2023–2025 and finds that greater tree canopy was associated with lower afternoon land-surface temperatures after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density [S1][S2]. Impervious surface was the strongest single predictor, followed by canopy cover; July heat-related emergency calls were 23% higher in the hottest neighborhood quartile than in the coolest [S3]. The brief recommends prioritizing tree planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035, estimating 6,000 street trees would cost about $2.1 million over ten years [S4]. output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, reports a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It finds that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon land-surface temperature, accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief says the findings support a targeted planting program in the hottest neighborhoods. [S1]

Canopy cover was measured from 2024 aerial imagery and ranged from 6% to 41% across the neighborhoods. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. The analysis used a multiple regression model with average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors. [S2]

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C; Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C—a difference of 6.4°C. The brief identifies share of impervious surface as the strongest single predictor of surface temperature and canopy cover as the second strongest. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile. [S3]

The brief notes that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design shows association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The estimated cost of planting 6,000 street trees is about $2.1 million over ten years. [S4]

output.detailed_summary:
The research brief, dated September 2026, describes a study of 48 Riverton neighborhoods between 2023 and 2025. It reports that each 10-percentage-point increase in tree canopy cover was associated with a 1.4°C lower average afternoon surface temperature, after accounting for impervious surfaces and building density. The brief presents this finding as support for a targeted planting program in the hottest neighborhoods [S1].

For its methods, the study measured tree canopy from 2024 aerial imagery; canopy cover ranged from 6% to 41%. Land-surface temperature (LST) was derived from 36 cloud-free satellite passes in July of 2023, 2024 and 2025, all between 1:00 and 3:00 p.m. A multiple regression model used average afternoon LST as the outcome and canopy cover, share of impervious surface, and building density as predictors [S2].

Eastgate, with 6% canopy, was the hottest neighborhood, averaging 41.2°C. Willow Park, with 41% canopy, was the coolest, averaging 34.8°C—a difference of 6.4°C. The share of impervious surface was the strongest single predictor of surface temperature, followed by canopy cover. Heat-related emergency calls during July were 23% higher in the hottest quartile of neighborhoods than in the coolest quartile [S3].

The brief notes that LST is not the same as the air temperature people experience, that the cross-sectional design establishes association rather than causation, and that the 2024 imagery may not reflect trees planted since then. It recommends prioritizing planting in Eastgate and Millbrook and setting a citywide target of 30% canopy cover by 2035. The estimated cost of planting 6,000 street trees is about $2.1 million over ten years [S4].
